trial_name: BaSICS — Infusion Rate: Effect of Slower vs Faster Intravenous Fluid Bolus Rates on Mortality in Critically Ill Patients
citation: Zampieri FG, Machado FR, Biondi RS, Freitas FGR, Veiga VC, Figueiredo RC, et al. Effect of slower vs faster intravenous fluid bolus rates on mortality in critically ill patients: the BaSICS randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2021;326(9):830-838
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, pragmatic, factorial, open-label for rate, double-blind for fluid type
one_liner: In ICU patients, slowing fluid boluses from 999 mL/h to 333 mL/h did not reduce 90-day mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96–1.11, P=0.46) and provided no kidney benefit.

pico.population: Critically ill ICU patients requiring crystalloid fluid challenges and having ≥1 risk factor for worse outcomes
pico.intervention: Slower bolus rate: 333 mL/h (500 mL over ~90 minutes) via infusion pump
pico.comparison: Faster bolus rate: 999 mL/h (500 mL over ~30 minutes) via infusion pump
pico.outcome: 90-day mortality; kidney replacement therapy within 90 days; organ dysfunction (SOFA score)

background.existing_knowledge: Fluid challenges are a foundational ICU intervention; previous evidence focused on type and volume of fluid, not rate. The FENICE cohort documented wide practice variation: 25th percentile infusion rate ~500 mL/h.
background.knowledge_gap: No large pragmatic ICU RCT had assessed whether infusion rate influences patient-centred outcomes.
background.hypothesis: Slower bolus infusion rates would reduce 90-day mortality and organ dysfunction/AKI (target HR ~0.90).

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, investigator-initiated, pragmatic 2×2 factorial trial comparing infusion rate (open-label) and fluid type (double-blind).
methods.setting: 75 ICUs in Brazil; enrolment May 2017–March 2020; follow-up completed October 2020.

inclusion: Clinician decision to administer a crystalloid fluid challenge for volume expansion
≥1 risk factor for worse outcomes (not fully enumerated)
exclusion: Concurrent enrolment in another clinical trial

methods.intervention: Slower bolus rate: 333 mL/h (typically 500 mL over ~90 minutes) via infusion pump; 500 mL of assigned crystalloid per challenge; safety allowance for faster delivery in emergencies.
methods.comparison: Faster bolus rate: 999 mL/h (typically 500 mL over ~30 minutes) via infusion pump; same volume and emergency discretion.
methods.blinding: Infusion rate unblinded (pragmatic pump setting); fluid type double-blind (identical masked study fluids). Primary outcome (mortality) objective.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 11,000 patients to detect HR 0.90 for 90-day mortality (assumed 35% mortality) with 89% power at two-sided α 0.05; interim analyses at 25%, 50%, 75% recruitment and early 1,000-patient safety review.
secondary_outcomes: Acute kidney failure requiring renal replacement therapy within 90 days
Day 3 SOFA total score and organ-specific components
methods.follow_up: 90 days for primary outcome; organ outcomes assessed at days 3 and 7, and up to 28 days for ventilation-free days.

headline_bullets: No significant difference in 90-day mortality: 26.6% (slower) vs 27.0% (faster); HR 1.03 (95% CI 0.96–1.11; P=0.46).
Renal replacement therapy within 90 days similar: RR 0.95 (95% CI 0.83–1.09); in-hospital KRT OR 0.92 (0.80–1.06).

Day 3 SOFA total score showed minimal difference (−0.10; 95% CI −0.21 to −0.01), with mixed organ component effects (cardiovascular and respiratory favoured slower rate; coagulation favoured faster rate).
Modest separation in day-1 fluid volume: 1162 mL (slower) vs 1252 mL (faster); absolute difference 90 mL.
No interaction between infusion rate and fluid type for mortality (P=0.98).

outcomes_table.note: Primary end point; mixed-effects Cox model adjusted for age, baseline SOFA, admission type, site as random effect; mITT after excluding post-randomisation consent withdrawals and duplicates.
Rate ratio; denominator is follow-up time (thousands of patient-days)

domains.notes: Central web-based randomisation; random permuted blocks of 12; stratified by centre and factorial assignment; robust concealment.
Rate allocation open-label; primary outcome (mortality) objective but secondary outcomes (e.g., KRT initiation) potentially biased by group awareness.
Modified ITT after excluding 532 patients (lack of consent n=486, duplicate enrolment n=46) from 11,052 randomised; primary outcome missing in 25 patients, 15 imputed; overall low missingness.

Exposure contrast defined by pump rates; emergency deviations permitted but frequency not reported. Day-1 fluid volume difference modest (90 mL), suggesting limited separation in cumulative early fluid exposure.
Groups well matched: median age 61, APACHE II 17, baseline SOFA 4, sepsis ~26%, invasive ventilation ~38%, vasopressors ~13%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong for the mortality comparison due to robust randomisation, low missingness, and objective primary outcome; weaker for clinician-mediated secondary outcomes because of open-label rate allocation and modest exposure separation.

domains.notes: Large pragmatic cohort (Brazil) with mixed admission types (planned surgery 44%, unplanned non-sepsis 29%, sepsis 26%), moderate severity (APACHE II 17), applicable to many general ICUs.

Relevant where fluid challenges are pump-delivered; less applicable when boluses are given by pressure bag/manual push (>999 mL/h) or during early ED/pre-hospital resuscitation. Not tested in the earliest hours of septic shock outside ICU.

external_validity.verdict: Findings are highly generalisable to ICU fluid challenges delivered by pump over ~30–90 minutes, but less so for early resuscitation contexts or bolus speeds outside the tested range.

strengths: Rigorous mixed-effects modelling accounting for centre clustering
Factorial design allowed assessment of interaction with fluid type (P=0.98)
limitations: Post-randomisation exclusions for lack of consent and duplicate enrolment (532 of 11,052)
Modest separation in day-1 cumulative fluid volume (90 mL difference)
Emergency deviations from assigned rate permitted but frequency not reported
‘Faster’ arm limited to pump rate (999 mL/h) and may not represent common pressure-bag bolus practice
Intervention starts in ICU, not early ED resuscitation

critical_appraisal.summary: BaSICS-rate is a large, well-conducted pragmatic RCT demonstrating that slowing fluid boluses from 999 to 333 mL/h does not alter mortality or kidney outcomes in a general ICU population; the open-label design and modest exposure separation weaken inference for clinician-mediated endpoints.
strengths: Objective primary outcome with minimal missing data
weaknesses: Unblinded rate could bias secondary outcomes
Limited biologic separation in early fluid delivery may dilute true rate effect

sections.authors_conclusion: Slowing fluid bolus infusion rate from 999 mL/h to 333 mL/h did not reduce 90-day mortality or improve kidney outcomes in ICU patients; bolus rate within this pump-driven range is not a major outcome modifier.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine slowing of fluid boluses to 333 mL/h does not change mortality or need for renal support. Emphasise bolus indication, reassessment, and avoiding unnecessary fluids over manipulating pump rate within the 30–90 minute window.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients receiving pump-delivered crystalloid fluid challenges of 500 mL; general medical, surgical, and sepsis patients.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not imply that any rate is equally safe; very rapid boluses (>999 mL/h) or very slow infusions were not tested, nor was early pre-ICU resuscitation.
implementation_caveats: May not apply when bolus given by pressure bag or manual push.
Intervention began in ICU, not in the emergency department.
Emergency deviations allowed; clinicians should continue to use clinical judgement.

controversies.topic: Editorial conclusion on rate and composition
controversies.notes: Editorial concluded neither crystalloid composition nor infusion rate meaningfully affected 90-day mortality in BaSICS, and that small day-3 SOFA signal has uncertain clinical relevance given mixed component directions.

The tested contrast (333 vs 999 mL/h) reflects infusion-pump constraints and may not address the real-world scenario of pressure-bag ‘rapid bolus’, raising concern about under-separation for truly rapid infusion.
Observed practice variation in FENICE highlights that ‘rate’ is entangled with clinician reassessment and subsequent fluid decisions, complicating interpretation of causal pathways.

controversies.topic: Context dependence from companion fluid type trial
controversies.notes: BaSICS fluid-type report found no overall mortality difference but a signal of harm in traumatic brain injury, reinforcing that fluid strategy effects may be context-dependent and rate findings should not be extrapolated to all phenotypes.

controversies.topic: Continued emphasis on other resuscitation targets
controversies.notes: Subsequent major trials (e.g., ANDROMEDA-SHOCK) focused on perfusion targets and fluid/vasopressor balance rather than bolus rate, showing no mortality benefit from peripheral perfusion–targeted resuscitation.

Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2016 emphasises early fluids and reassessment but provides limited specific infusion rate direction, consistent with BaSICS-rate demonstrating equipoise within common pump-based rates.

context_related_trials.relation: Documented wide practice variation in fluid challenge infusion rates, providing rationale for BaSICS-rate.
The other factorial intervention in the same study; found no overall mortality difference between balanced crystalloids and saline, with a potential harm signal in traumatic brain injury.
Illustrates that subsequent resuscitation research has prioritised perfusion targets and fluid/vasopressor balance over bolus rate, with similarly neutral mortality findings.

unresolved_questions: Does infusion rate matter during the earliest hours of septic shock outside ICU or when boluses are given by pressure bag (≥999 mL/h)?
Would further slowing (<333 mL/h) or faster rates (>999 mL/h) affect outcomes?
Is rate modification more impactful in subgroups with higher illness severity or specific phenotypes (e.g., right ventricular dysfunction)?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ICU patients, slowing fluid boluses from 999 to 333 mL/h didn’t change 90-day mortality or kidney outcomes; focus on whether to give a bolus, not how fast the pump runs.
